In a Password Spray Attack, the attacker tries one or two commonly used passwords (like Welcome123, Password1, Winter2024) across many usernames. This is different from brute-force because it avoids lockout protections that trigger after several wrong attempts on a single account. Password spraying is used against corporate portals, email logins, RDP servers, SMB, or any service that supports authentication. In this simulation, we’ll use hydra or crackmapexec on Kali Linux to spray a single password across many Windows domain users over SMB. text: Switch Spoofing (Trunk Spoofing) . category AI Agents & LLM Exploits . attack VLAN Hopping / Layer 2 Attack . In a Switch Spoofing Attack, the attacker connects a rogue system (like Kali Linux or a malicious switch) to a switch port configured for Dynamic Trunking Protocol (DTP). DTP is used to auto-negotiate trunking between switches. If the legitimate switch port is set to auto or dynamic desirable, the attacker's interface can trick it into creating a trunk port. As a result, the attacker gains access to multiple VLANs, violating network segmentation. This is a VLAN hopping technique and can lead to unauthorized access to otherwise isolated traffic. We simulate this using Kali Linux + Yersinia tool on a Cisco switch-enabled lab. target Managed switches with DTP-enabled ports . vulnerability Dynamic Trunking Protocol (DTP) negotiation enabled on access ports

text: Double Tagging Attack (802.1Q VLAN) . category AI Agents & LLM Exploits . attack VLAN Hopping / Layer 2 Evasion . In a Double Tagging Attack, an attacker in a VLAN (e.g., VLAN 10) crafts an Ethernet frame with two VLAN tags: an outer tag for their own VLAN, and an inner tag for the target VLAN (e.g., VLAN 20). Some misconfigured switches remove only the outer tag and then forward the frame based on the inner tag, effectively bypassing segmentation and delivering the packet into the victim VLAN. This is a VLAN hopping technique that requires no trunk access — only an access port and switch with improper VLAN filtering. We simulate this attack from Kali Linux using Scapy or manually crafted packets, then observe with Wireshark or the target’s response. target Layer 2 VLAN-enabled switches . vulnerability 802.1Q double-tagged frame + switch stripping only outer tag

text: Voice VLAN Injection Attack . category AI Agents & LLM Exploits . attack VLAN Hopping / Layer 2 Exploit . In many enterprise setups, VoIP phones are connected to a switch port, and PCs connect to the phone. The switch port is configured with a data VLAN (PC traffic) and a voice VLAN (for the phone). Switches often identify phones using LLDP or CDP (link-layer discovery protocols). Attackers connected to the same switch port can pretend to be an IP phone by forging LLDP/CDP frames, tricking the switch into giving them access to the voice VLAN, which may be less filtered or monitored. text: MAC Flooding + VLAN Cross-Talk Attack . category AI Agents & LLM Exploits . attack Layer 2 Table Overflow + VLAN Leakage . In this combined Layer 2 attack, an attacker first launches a MAC Flooding Attack by sending a huge number of fake MAC addresses into the switch using macof. This overflows the switch’s CAM table, making it forget which port is associated with which MAC address. As a result, the switch starts broadcasting frames to all ports, like a hub. If the switch is misconfigured or under load, it may start leaking frames between VLANs, causing VLAN Cross-Talk. This violates network segmentation and allows an attacker to capture sensitive data from VLANs they don’t belong to. It’s deadly in flat or poorly segmented networks. target VLAN-enabled Switches with CAM Table . vulnerability Limited CAM table size and lack of port securitySwitch not dropping VLAN-tagged frames properly

text: DNS Amplification DoS Attack . category AI Agents & LLM Exploits . attack Reflective Amplification + IP Spoofing . In this attack, the attacker sends small forged DNS queries to an open DNS resolver with the victim’s IP address spoofed. The attack is called “amplification” because the response is much larger (sometimes 70x) than the request. text: DNS Takeover via DHCPv6 Injection . category AI/ML Security . attack DNS Redirection via Rogue DHCPv6 Reply . This attack simulates a scenario where an attacker becomes a rogue DHCPv6 server on a LAN and sends forged DHCPv6 replies to victims. The victim unknowingly resolves domains through the attacker's server, enabling phishing, MITM, traffic logging, or malware injection. This simulation demonstrates how an attacker can bypass weak or misconfigured OSPF authentication to inject unauthorized LSAs or form rogue adjacencies with internal routers. OSPF supports various authentication modes: Null (none), Plaintext (simple password), and MD5. If OSPF is running with no auth or reused/shared simple passwords, attackers can easily inject fake LSAs, form neighbor relationships, or manipulate the routing table. This can lead to MITM, route hijacking, or blackhole attacks. This attack is effective in networks that expose OSPF interfaces on internal VLANs or lack strict access control. target Enterprise Core<brBranch Routers<brCampus Edge<brPublic Cloud VM routers . vulnerability - No OSPF authentication- Use of plaintext/simple password- Misconfigured router ACLs- Exposed interfaces

text: BGP Prefix Hijacking . category AI/ML Security . attack Routing Protocol Manipulation / Hijacking . This simulation illustrates how an attacker, with control over a malicious BGP-speaking router, can perform BGP prefix hijacking to falsely advertise ownership of IP prefixes belonging to another AS (Autonomous System). If upstream ISPs or IXPs (Internet Exchange Points) do not strictly filter BGP advertisements, the fake route can propagate globally, causing traffic to be rerouted, blackholed, or intercepted. This attack has been used in real-world incidents to hijack cryptocurrencies, perform surveillance, or disrupt service delivery. This is commonly simulated in BGP-enabled lab environments, ISPs, or cloud-based routers. target ISP Routers<brInternet Exchange Points<brCloud Gateways<brAutonomous Systems . vulnerability - Lack of prefix filtering- No RPKI/ROA validation- Acceptance of third-party prefix advertisements- Missing AS-PATH or prefix-list filters

text: Man-in-the-Middle via BGP Manipulation . category AI/ML Security . attack Routing Protocol Exploitation / MITM . This simulation shows how an attacker with access to a malicious BGP router (rogue ASN) can exploit the lack of route validation in BGP to reroute internet traffic through its own network, effectively performing a Man-in-the-Middle (MITM). By announcing IP prefixes belonging to a legitimate AS and advertising them with shorter or more specific paths, the attacker convinces upstream routers to send traffic through the rogue ASN. The attacker can then inspect, manipulate, or drop this traffic. text: BlueKeep (CVE-2019-0708) . category AI/ML Security . attack Remote Code Execution via RDP Vulnerability . BlueKeep is a critical Remote Code Execution (RCE) vulnerability in Microsoft’s Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) service, discovered in 2019. It affects older Windows versions like Windows 7, Server 2008, and XP, allowing an unauthenticated attacker to execute code remotely by sending crafted RDP packets before authentication. This can lead to wormable attacks, allowing malware to spread automatically from system to system (like WannaCry). text: PrintNightmare (CVE-2021-34527) . category AI/ML Security . attack Local/Remote Code Execution via Print Spooler . PrintNightmare is a critical Windows vulnerability affecting the Print Spooler service on many Windows versions. It allows remote and local attackers to execute arbitrary code with SYSTEM privileges, by abusing printer driver installation features over SMB or RPC. Even unprivileged domain users can exploit it to perform privilege escalation or remote code execution (RCE). The vulnerability lies in how the RpcAddPrinterDriverEx() function improperly validates input paths. An attacker can force the target to load a malicious DLL via network shares. text: MS08-067 (NetAPI Exploit) . category AI/ML Security . attack Remote Code Execution via SMB/NetAPI Buffer Overflow . MS08-067 is a critical remote code execution vulnerability in the Windows Server service (svchost.exe) due to a flaw in the handling of malformed RPC requests via SMB on port 445. It affects Windows XP, Server 2003, and Vista, and is wormable, allowing unauthenticated attackers to gain SYSTEM privileges remotely without any user interaction. It was the core vulnerability used by Conficker worm. The attacker sends a specially crafted RPC request to the vulnerable machine’s SMB service that overflows a buffer in NetAPI32.dll, allowing them to execute shellcode. This simulation demonstrates how a red teamer can exploit it using Metasploit in a lab setup. target Windows XP<brWindows Server 2003<brWindows Vista . vulnerability - Buffer overflow in NetAPI32.dll via SMB<br- Improper input validation on malformed RPC calls

text: Zerologon (CVE-2020-1472) . category AI/ML Security . attack Privilege Escalation / Domain Takeover via Netlogon . Zerologon is a critical privilege escalation vulnerability in the Netlogon Remote Protocol (MS-NRPC), affecting Windows Domain Controllers. It allows an unauthenticated attacker on the same network to impersonate the domain controller account by sending specially crafted Netlogon messages. This exploit abuses a cryptographic flaw where, due to improper use of AES-CFB8, an attacker can bypass authentication by sending all-zero challenge/responses. If successful, the attacker can reset the machine account password of the DC, perform full domain compromise, and impersonate any computer or user in Active Directory. target Windows Server 2012/2016/2019<brActive Directory Domain Controllers . vulnerability - AES-CFB8 cryptographic flaw in Netlogon authentication- Allows authentication bypass via all-zero challenge/response

text: Dirty COW (CVE-2016-5195) – Local Kernel Exploit . category AI/ML Security . attack Privilege Escalation (Local – Linux Kernel) . Dirty COW is a critical local privilege escalation vulnerability in the Linux kernel’s memory subsystem, specifically in the handling of the copy-on-write (COW) mechanism. The flaw allows an unprivileged local user to write to read-only memory mappings, thereby overwriting system files (like /etc/passwd) or binaries they normally should not have access to. Exploiting Dirty COW lets attackers gain root privileges by modifying files in memory they should only be able to read. It was present in almost all major Linux distributions and kernel versions prior to 4.8.3. This simulation demonstrates how to escalate from a regular user to root using a well-known Dirty COW exploit. target Linux desktops<brLinux servers<brCloud VMs with shell access . vulnerability - Race condition in Linux kernel memory management- copy-on-write (COW) improperly handled when writing to read-only files

text: Kernel Stack/Heap Overflow Exploits . category AI/ML Security . attack Local Privilege Escalation / Remote RCE (Kernel) . Stack and heap overflows in kernel-mode drivers or system calls are serious vulnerabilities that can lead to privilege escalation or full system compromise. These exploits overwrite data structures or return addresses in kernel memory space by sending malicious input from user space. Often used in CVE-based exploits, such as those in win32k.sys (Windows) or custom vulnerable drivers in CTFs and red team labs. text: Sticky Broadcast Abuse . category AI/ML Security . attack Broadcast Manipulation / Unauthorized Component Trigger . In Android, Sticky Broadcasts are special types of broadcasts that stay in memory even after they are sent. This allows components (like Broadcast Receivers) to access the last broadcasted data even if they weren’t active at the time the broadcast was sent. While deprecated in newer Android versions, many legacy apps still use sendStickyBroadcast(). If a sticky broadcast is not protected with permissions or validation, a malicious app or ADB user can inject fake data using a sticky broadcast, and any component that listens for it will receive the malicious payload and react to it. This can result in unintended behaviors, logic bypass, or privilege escalation, such as spoofing system status, injecting fake app events, or forcing internal workflows. target Android App (APK) . vulnerability Unprotected use of sticky broadcasts

solution: Never use sticky broadcasts in production; if used, apply android:permission; verify intent origin in receiver code and sanitize all inputs
impact: Persistent logic injection, spoofed states, unauthorized feature access, bypassed flows
title: Sticky Broadcast Abuse

text: Implicit Intent Hijack (Component Confusion) . category AI/ML Security . attack Intent Hijacking / Component Confusion . Android apps often use implicit intents to request actions like opening a file, sharing content, launching a camera, or downloading data. When an implicit intent is sent, Android looks for the best-matching app component (Activity, Service, etc.) to handle it. If a malicious app registers a matching intent filter, it can intercept or hijack the intent, tricking the system into launching the malicious component instead of the intended one. This is called Component Confusion or Implicit Intent Hijacking, and it can lead to data theft, phishing UI, spoofed responses, or malicious payload injection. target Android App (APK) . vulnerability Implicit Intents sent without specifying trusted component

solution: Always use explicit intents when launching internal components; validate component origin and use package restrictions; don’t expose sensitive data via unprotected implicit intents
impact: Hijack of legitimate system or app workflow, data theft, phishing UI, spoofed response injection
title: Implicit Intent Hijack (Component Confusion)

text: Unvalidated file:// URL Loaded from User Input . category AI/ML Security . attack Local File Inclusion via WebView . Android apps often embed a WebView to load content like help pages, documentation, or URLs based on user input. If the app loads URLs directly from unvalidated user input (like from an intent extra, deep link, or form field) and does not restrict to trusted domains or schemes, an attacker can pass a file:// URI instead of a safe https:// one. This leads the WebView to load local files from the app or system — a Local File Inclusion (LFI). This is known as WebView LFI via file://, and can expose sensitive files like cookies, source code, or cached data. target Android App (APK) . vulnerability WebView loading file:// URLs without validation

title: Unvalidated file:// URL Loaded from User Input

text: JavaScript-Enabled LFI + Local File JS Execution . category AI/ML Security . attack Local File Inclusion + Script Injection via WebView . Many Android apps embed a WebView to show help content, user-submitted links, or files. If the app allows user input to control the URL or file path loaded in WebView without validating the source, and has JavaScript enabled, an attacker can load a malicious local file using the file:// scheme. If that file contains JavaScript, it will be executed in the app’s context, which may lead to XSS (cross-site scripting), data theft, cookie access, or visual phishing. This attack is real and widespread in apps that call webView.loadUrl(...) using untrusted data and set webView.getSettings().setJavaScriptEnabled(true). target Android App (APK) . vulnerability Loading file:// URI from untrusted source + JS enabled

text: Accessing content:// URIs via WebView (LFI using Content Providers) . category AI/ML Security . attack Local File Inclusion via WebView + Content URI Access . Android uses content:// URIs to access data from Content Providers, which are used to share files, messages, databases, or media between apps. Normally, only specific apps have permission to access a given content:// URI. But if an app's WebView accepts and loads unvalidated URIs from user input, and if JavaScript is enabled, an attacker can load a content:// URI and attempt to steal data or trigger actions in other apps. Some apps expose exported or insecure content providers (android:exported="true") that can be accessed directly using URIs like content://com.example.app.provider/userdata. If the vulnerable app does not block content:// scheme, this becomes a Local File Inclusion attack via WebView that exposes sensitive internal or inter-app data. target Android App (APK) . vulnerability Unvalidated content:// URI loading in WebView + exposed Content Providers

text: Reading App-Private Files via Path Traversal in WebView . category AI/ML Security . attack Local File Inclusion (LFI) + Path Traversal . Some Android apps allow users to specify file paths or file names (e.g., for opening help docs, loading reports, exporting files, etc.) via WebView or file-based features. If the app does not sanitize the input path and passes it directly to WebView or a file loader, an attacker can perform a path traversal using sequences like ../ to move out of the allowed folder and access private files in the app’s internal storage. If the app also allows file:// URLs to be loaded in WebView, and JavaScript is enabled, this attack can even lead to JS-based data theft. This vulnerability is often overlooked because apps assume users won't manipulate file paths, but in reality, WebView combined with file:// + ../ can read shared_prefs, SQLite DBs, cached files, etc. target Android App (APK) . vulnerability WebView loading file:// URLs with unsanitized user-controlled file paths

title: Reading App-Private Files via Path Traversal in WebView

text: Intent-Based File Inclusion via Deep Link . category AI/ML Security . attack Local File Inclusion (LFI) via Deep Link + WebView . Many Android apps register deep links (special links like appname://open) to allow launching specific features directly via a browser or intent. These deep links often contain parameters (e.g., appname://open?file=report.html). If the app’s WebView or file loader takes these parameters and directly loads them without sanitizing, it’s possible to inject a file:// path or use ../ traversal to read sensitive internal or external files. This becomes an LFI (Local File Inclusion) triggered through an intent or a deep link, allowing attackers to include and read arbitrary files inside the WebView — even without touching the app's UI. This attack is extremely common in apps that support file preview, report download, or offline content rendering through URLs or filenames from deep links. target Android App (APK) . vulnerability WebView + Deep Link Intent loading unsanitized file paths

text: Using JavaScript Interface to Exfiltrate Local Files . category AI/ML Security . attack Local File Inclusion (LFI) + JavaScriptInterface Abuse . Android WebView allows apps to expose Java objects into JavaScript using addJavascriptInterface(). If the app uses this interface to expose sensitive functions (like file access, logging, or intents) to any webpage loaded inside the WebView — and if the app also loads untrusted or attacker-controlled HTML via file:// or deep links — the attacker can use JavaScript to call those functions. When combined with LFI (such as loading local files via file://), the attacker can inject a malicious HTML that uses the JavaScript interface to exfiltrate internal app files, such as shared preferences, user info, or DB contents. This is highly dangerous, especially when apps do not restrict WebView content sources or JS interface binding. target Android App (APK) . vulnerability WebView loading file:// content + Exposed addJavascriptInterface()

text: Remote Code Execution via Known SDK Vulnerability . category AI/ML Security . attack RCE via Outdated Third-Party SDK . Many Android applications use third-party SDKs (for ads, analytics, social login, etc.) that come as .aar or .jar files. If an app includes an outdated version of an SDK with known vulnerabilities, attackers can exploit those flaws to achieve Remote Code Execution (RCE), especially when the SDK exposes JavaScript bridges, insecure web content loading, or insecure file parsing. A well-known real-world example is the Cordova Android Plugin Vulnerability (CVE-2017-3160), which allowed JavaScript code running in WebView to execute arbitrary Java code via an insecure addJavascriptInterface() in an outdated Cordova WebView plugin. target Android App (APK) . vulnerability Insecure outdated SDK with vulnerable JavaScript interface or input handling

A mobile application uses outdated OpenSSL/TLS libraries that lack support for secure protocols or have known vulnerabilities. This allows an attacker on the same network (e.g., public Wi-Fi) to intercept, decrypt, and possibly modify sensitive user data such as login credentials or API keys during transmission, even if the app claims to use HTTPS. target Mobile Apps (Android/iOS) . vulnerability Outdated SSL/TLS Library (OpenSSL)

This becomes critical when SDKs send such data to external servers over HTTP or without encryption, leading to major privacy breaches. text: WebView RCE via Third-Party Plugin (Cordova/Capacitor) . category AI/ML Security . attack Remote Code Execution (RCE) via Plugin Injection . Hybrid mobile apps (using frameworks like Apache Cordova, Ionic Capacitor, or PhoneGap) allow JavaScript-based app development using WebView. These frameworks use plugins to bridge native functionality (like file access, camera, etc.) to JavaScript. If outdated or misconfigured, plugins like cordova-plugin-inappbrowser, cordova-plugin-file, or cordova-plugin-customurlscheme can expose dangerous native features to attacker-controlled JavaScript via exec() or postMessage() functions. This can lead to full Remote Code Execution (RCE) via WebView. text: Crash / DoS via Glide / ImageView Bug . category AI/ML Security . attack Application Denial of Service (DoS) via Resource Exhaustion . Many Android apps use the Glide image loading library to efficiently display images from remote URLs. However, outdated versions of Glide (e.g., before v4.11) or misused ImageView implementations can cause crashes or ANRs (App Not Responding) when loading malicious image payloads. A very large image file (e.g., 8000x8000 pixels or more), a specially crafted corrupt image, or an endless redirect loop can lead to memory exhaustion or infinite processing loops, crashing the app instantly or freezing it permanently. This can be used for DoS attacks, crashing the app every time it opens or even triggering a reboot loop in some cases. target Mobile Apps using Glide or ImageView . vulnerability Glide Image Loader Memory Exhaustion, Corrupt Image Processing

text: GSON Deserialization RCE . category AI/ML Security . attack Remote Code Execution (RCE) via Insecure Deserialization . GSON is a widely used Java/Android library for converting JSON into Java objects. In older or misconfigured versions (especially before v2.8.9), if an app deserializes untrusted JSON into generic Object types (e.g., TypeToken<Object>), or allows polymorphic deserialization using attacker-controlled types, it can result in RCE. Attackers can send specially crafted JSON payloads that force GSON to instantiate dangerous gadget classes (e.g., from the app itself or from included libraries like Apache Commons), eventually leading to execution of arbitrary code. This is particularly dangerous in mobile apps with API endpoints or local WebView bridges that accept JSON and parse them using GSON without strict type enforcement. target Mobile Apps using GSON for JSON Parsing . vulnerability Insecure Deserialization via GSON TypeToken or Polymorphic Objects

text: Exposure to Known CVEs in PlayCore, ExoPlayer, Firebase . category AI/ML Security . attack Exploitation via Known Vulnerable SDK Versions . Android apps often use Google libraries such as Play Core (used for dynamic feature delivery), ExoPlayer (for video streaming), and Firebase (for analytics, authentication, etc.). For example, CVE-2020-8913 in Play Core allowed attackers to load arbitrary code from untrusted sources, and CVE-2021-0339 in ExoPlayer allowed memory corruption. text: Abuse of ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION on Android . category AI/ML Security . attack Privacy Violation / Stealth Location Tracking . An Android application requests ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION permission to collect user location data even when the app is not actively in use. A malicious Android app uses a Foreground Service to hide the fact that it's collecting the user's location in real-time. Foreground services appear legitimate to Android (e.g., displaying a media player or fitness tracking), so they bypass many background location restrictions. This attack tricks the user into thinking the app is doing something helpful (like step tracking or music playing) while secretly collecting and sending GPS data to a remote server or attacker-controlled endpoint. target Android App . vulnerability Abuse of Foreground Service and Location APIs

text: Third-Party SDKs Collecting Location Without Transparency . category AI/ML Security . attack Supply Chain / Covert Location Tracking . In this scenario, a seemingly harmless mobile app integrates a third-party SDK (Software Development Kit) from an analytics or ad network. This SDK silently collects the user’s precise GPS location even when the app is not being used, and sends it to external servers. The app developer may not be aware of the SDK's full data behavior, or may include it knowingly for monetization. This is a supply chain privacy abuse because the app itself doesn’t directly request or use location data — the third-party SDK inside it does. target Android App . vulnerability Hidden Location Harvesting via 3rd-Party SDK

text: Bluetooth Beacons or Wi-Fi SSID Logging . category AI/ML Security . attack Passive Location Tracking Without GPS . In this attack, a malicious mobile application collects environmental signals (nearby Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) beacons and Wi-Fi SSID names). These identifiers are often location-specific (e.g., “Starbucks_123” or “Office_WIFI_2F”), so collecting them allows an attacker to infer the user’s current location, even when location permissions like GPS are not granted. Since scanning for Bluetooth and Wi-Fi is possible without fine-grained location permissions on many Android versions, users may never know their location is being monitored. Attackers can compare scanned SSIDs against known public or commercial location databases (like Google’s or Apple’s) to get GPS coordinates. target Android App . vulnerability Radio Signal-Based Location Tracking

This breaches privacy and enables long-term tracking. mitre T1614 - System Location Discovery

text: Continuous Location Upload via AlarmManager or WorkManager . category AI/ML Security . attack Persistent Background Location Logging . This attack simulates how a malicious app can schedule continuous GPS location uploads using Android’s AlarmManager or WorkManager. These APIs are designed for task scheduling like reminders, periodic updates, or background syncing. However, an attacker can abuse them to collect a user’s location at frequent intervals (every few minutes or hours) even if the user is not using the app or has forgotten about it. Since AlarmManager can work during device idle state (with some restrictions on Android 6+), and WorkManager is optimized for persistent background tasks, both can be exploited for silent surveillance. This attack targets mobile apps that store authentication tokens, session IDs, API keys, or user credentials in plaintext in local storage files like SharedPreferences on Android or NSUserDefaults on iOS. If an attacker gets physical access to a mobile device that is not encrypted or is already unlocked, they can extract these files using simple tools like ADB (Android) or Filza/SSH (iOS Jailbroken). Once extracted, the attacker can read these tokens, replay sessions, impersonate the user, or call internal APIs without login. This is common when developers forget to encrypt sensitive data before storing it locally. target Android and iOS apps storing sensitive data in local app storage . vulnerability Tokens and secrets stored in plaintext inside app sandbox without encryption

detection: File system integrity checks, code audit, static analysis of shared_prefs/plists, token scope audits

impact: Account takeover, unauthorized API access, impersonation, bypass login
title: Tokens in Plaintext in SharedPreferences / UserDefaults

text: No Biometrics = Direct App Access . category AI/ML Security . attack Stolen Device Attack (App Bypass due to No Biometrics) . This attack targets Android or iOS phones that do not use biometric authentication (fingerprint or face) to lock individual sensitive apps such as banking apps, email, messaging apps, or password managers. When a phone is lost or stolen, and the screen lock is weak (or the device is already unlocked), the attacker can directly open these apps and access private data because there is no biometric or PIN required at the app level. Many apps support optional biometric locks, but users often skip enabling them, relying only on device screen lock — which, once bypassed or unlocked, exposes everything inside the apps. This leads to complete compromise of personal data, financial details, or even email recovery and social media hijack. target Unlocked or unattended Android/iOS smartphones with no app-level biometric protection . vulnerability Lack of biometric enforcement in sensitive apps even after device unlock

impact: Full access to emails, bank data, private chats, UPI IDs, account recovery, saved passwords
title: No Biometrics = Direct App Access

text: SD Card Access (Android) . category AI/ML Security . attack Stolen Device Attack (External Storage Exploitation) . This attack targets Android phones that use a physical SD card to store photos, documents, app backups, WhatsApp media, exported notes, or even sensitive databases. If the device is lost or stolen, the attacker can simply remove the SD card, insert it into another phone or laptop, and read all the files — even if the phone is locked or powered off, because SD cards are not encrypted by default on most Android devices. Many apps (like WhatsApp, backup tools, or custom file managers) allow storing sensitive information on external storage, assuming the user knows the risks — but attackers take advantage of this poor protection to quickly copy and exploit private data. target Android phones using SD cards (with sensitive app/media data stored externally) . vulnerability No encryption of SD card contents; app data and media stored in plaintext on removable storage

title: SD Card Access (Android)

text: Session Token Theft via File Copy . category AI/ML Security . attack Stolen Device Attack (File-Based Session Hijack) . This attack targets Android or iOS devices where mobile apps store session tokens (auth tokens, cookies, JWTs) in local unprotected files such as SharedPreferences, SQLite databases, or app cache. If a device is lost or stolen and not fully encrypted, an attacker can use tools like ADB (Android) or SSH/Filza (iOS Jailbroken) to copy those files, extract the tokens, and reuse them to access the victim’s account without a password. Tokens are often long-lived and reused silently in API calls. If the app does not bind tokens to device ID, IP, or refresh frequently, stolen tokens can be reused on another phone or system easily. target Android or iOS apps storing session tokens insecurely . vulnerability Unencrypted, persistent session tokens stored in readable files

title: Session Token Theft via File Copy

However, due to misconfiguration, the files themselves are accessible publicly even if the bucket itself is not listable. This means anyone with a direct link can download the file, just like clicking on a public download link, without logging in or using any credentials. text: Use Exposed Files to Pivot . category AI/ML Security . attack Misconfigured S3 / Blob Storage Attacks . text: Hardcoded JWT Secrets . category AI/ML Security . attack Exposed Secrets in Code . Many web developers use JSON Web Tokens (JWT) for authentication. JWTs are signed with a secret (e.g., HMAC SHA256 using a secret string). If the secret is hardcoded in source code (e.g., in config.js, auth.py, .env, or app.js) and pushed to public GitHub repositories, attackers can use it to forge valid JWT tokens, impersonate admin users, bypass authentication, and take over accounts. This is especially dangerous when access control is based only on the JWT signature and not verified against a server-side database. target Web Applications using JWT . vulnerability Hardcoded authentication secrets inside code/config files
event_text: security event Hardcoded JWT Secrets detected by JWT tampering detection, code review, JWT signature verification logs, GitHub secret scanning impact Account takeover, admin privilege escalation, authentication bypass mitre T1552.001 (Credentials in Files)
label: exploit_injection
detection: JWT tampering detection, code review, JWT signature verification logs, GitHub secret scanning
solution: ✅ Never hardcode JWT secrets in source code✅ Use secure .env files and vaults for secrets✅ Use strong, random secrets (32+ chars)✅ Rotate secrets regularly✅ Add exp claim in JWTs to expire old tokens✅ Implement RBAC and server-side checks (not just JWT roles)
impact: Account takeover, admin privilege escalation, authentication bypass
title: Hardcoded JWT Secrets

text: OAuth Client ID / Secret . category AI/ML Security . attack Exposed OAuth Credentials . Many applications use OAuth 2.0 to authenticate users via third-party identity providers like Google, GitHub, Facebook, etc. Developers must register an "OAuth App" with the provider, which gives them a Client ID and a Client Secret. The secret is like a password and should never be exposed. However, developers often accidentally leak the client_id and client_secret in frontend JavaScript code, mobile apps, public GitHub repos, or .env files. If exposed, attackers can impersonate the app, steal authorization tokens, or conduct phishing attacks using fake login flows. target OAuth-enabled Web & Mobile Apps . vulnerability Exposed Client Credentials in Repositories or App Code

text: Firebase Storage with Wildcard Read/Write Rules (read: true, write: true) . category AI/ML Security . attack Unauthenticated Data Exposure & Arbitrary Write . In this scenario, a mobile or web app developer configures Firebase Storage with rules like read: true and write: true to make development easier. This configuration allows anyone on the internet to read all files stored in Firebase (including user data, ID cards, invoices, private content) and write any file, including malware or fake files. These rules, when publicly exposed, turn the storage into an open data bucket that attackers can easily abuse without even needing an account or authentication. This misconfiguration is shockingly common in real-world apps and leads to sensitive data leaks, brand damage, and malware distribution. target Firebase Storage . vulnerability Public Read/Write Access due to Rules Misconfiguration (read: true, write: true)

In this scenario, a developer or admin creates an IAM user in AWS and attaches the AmazonS3FullAccess policy to that user. text: Lambda Function Access via Role Escalation . category AI/ML Security . attack Privilege Escalation via Over-Permissive IAM . In this scenario, an IAM user has limited permissions but is mistakenly granted the ability to attach roles or assume roles due to over-permissive IAM policies. The attacker discovers that they can escalate privileges by assuming a role attached to a Lambda function that has powerful permissions (e.g., admin, S3 full access, or even STS full access). By exploiting AWS Lambda’s attached roles and permissions structure, the attacker gains access far beyond their original user permissions. This happens when IAM users are allowed to run sts:AssumeRole, lambda:GetFunctionConfiguration, or iam:PassRole with overly broad resource access (e.g., using "Resource": "*"), or when Lambda functions themselves use high-privileged execution roles. target AWS Lambda . vulnerability IAM role escalation via over-permissive trust relationships and pass role permissions

text: GCP IAM Key With Editor Role in Mobile App . category AI/ML Security . attack Cloud Account Takeover via Leaked Editor Role Key . In this real scenario, a mobile application (Android or iOS) accidentally includes a Google Cloud IAM service account key in the app package. Worse, this key belongs to a service account with the over-permissive “Editor” role (roles/editor). The Editor role allows full control over most GCP resources: reading, writing, creating, deleting, or even modifying IAM policies. When an attacker extracts this key by reverse-engineering the mobile app, they can use it to impersonate the service account, explore the environment, and take control of the project or resources such as Cloud Storage, Firestore, Compute, and even Cloud Functions. This misconfiguration is extremely dangerous and commonly reported in mobile app bug bounties. target Google Cloud Platform (GCP) . vulnerability Leaked GCP Service Account Key with Over-Permissive Editor Role

text: Image Fetch via URL in Mobile App (Classic SSRF) . category AI/ML Security . attack Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) . In this real-world case, a mobile application has an image upload feature or URL preview function where the user can submit an external image URL. However, the app fails to validate the URL properly, allowing an attacker to point the URL to internal IPs or cloud metadata servers (like AWS EC2 Metadata URL or GCP metadata). text: QR Code or URL Preview via API (Blind SSRF) . category AI/ML Security . attack Blind Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) . In this scenario, a web or mobile API accepts a user-supplied URL and generates a preview card, summary, or QR code using server-side logic. The result is not directly shown, or only metadata is returned, making it a blind SSRF. An attacker uses this feature to make the backend server connect to internal services (metadata IPs, internal admin panels, etc.).
